topic: Robotics and the space physical clock under S4 'Embodied' (S3 Recursive cognition plus general-purpose robotics at scale): gate-by-gate compression of the Space Unlock Tree's physical gates by 2031 and 2035, factory-automation evidence from SpaceX, Rocket Lab, Relativity, Firefly and others, and whether a robots-build-robots loop matters by 2031 versus 2035

scenario_definition.S4_Embodied: S3 Recursive cognition (cognitive work 20-50x faster from 2029) plus general-purpose robots (humanoid and mobile-manipulator class, foundation-model controlled) deployed at scale in factories, labs, test sites, construction and off Earth, including robots helping build robots.
scenario_definition.what_S3_already_assumes: AI-run test stands and factories with physical multipliers ~1.3-1.5x (graph-v5.json domains.physclock.tables, 'Gate compression multipliers').
scenario_definition.what_S4_adds: Robotic labor that is 24/7, parallelizable and cheap, so labor-bound steps compress further and throughput-bound gates (capacity, replicates, facility queues, construction crews) become capital-bound. It does not change physics time constants, statistical evidence requirements, orbital mechanics, or institutional clocks.
scenario_definition.method: Each physical slice of the model's Amdahl table is split into labor-bound, physics-bound and institution/supply-bound sub-shares (estimates), calibrated so the S3 sub-multipliers reproduce the model's S3 slice speedups (fab 1.3x, I&T 1.5x, qualification 1.5x, launch 1.0x) and the 51% S3 ceiling. S4 then raises only the multipliers robotics can plausibly move by 2031 and by 2035. Calendar-time factor = fraction of today's duration (0.6x = 40% shorter).

key_findings: Robotics compresses throughput, not latency. It removes labor-bound time (setup, assembly, tending, inspection, construction crews) and turns capacity and replicate-statistics gates into capital problems, but it does not shorten a thermal-vacuum plateau, a 10,000-hour creep test, a hot-fire failure discovery, a flight-count reliability demonstration, a 26-month Mars window, or a statutory review.

S4 adds modestly to S3 by 2031. The new-program Amdahl ceiling moves from ~51% shorter (S3) to ~57-63% shorter (2.3-2.7x) in 2031 and ~66-74% (2.9-3.9x) in 2035. Realized values: ~40-50% shorter by 2031 (vs 35-45% S3) and ~50-62% by 2035, after adoption lag and robotic-process requalification.

There is a hard physical floor. Even with infinite cognition and infinite robots, the physics-, statistics- and institution-bound remainder caps compression of a new space program at ~78% shorter (~4.6x). Infinite cognition without robots stops at ~52% (2.1x), so robots roughly double the headroom but cannot remove the floor.

Factory automation in space has repeatedly sped up a step by large factors without moving cadence comparably. Rocket Lab's Rosie robot cut Electron composite processing from 400+ hours to 12 (~33x, Nov 2019), against a goal of one Electron every 7 days; Electron flew a record 21 launches in 2025 (one every ~17 days). Relativity's 95%-printed-parts approach yielded one failed orbital attempt and a pivot to conventional aluminum because printing domes was too slow for rate. Firefly's 2020 automated-composites plan (24 Alpha a year) coexists with roughly 1-3 launches a year through 2026. Rocket Lab's 90-tonne AFP robot (150,000+ hours projected saving) did not prevent Neutron slipping to NET Q4 2026.

Where automation already works, the gate has moved to launch. SpaceX Redmond averaged ~70 Starlink satellites/week (Dec 2025-Apr 2026, ~3,640/yr) and terminals reached ~200,000/week (S-1), while V3 deployment waits on Starship, which flew 5 times in 2025 and 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7. Starship hulls were in production through at least Ship 48 in Apr 2026, before V3's first flight; vehicle output is ahead of flight cadence.

Launch cadence is the master variable for statistics-bound gates. A 0.99/90% zero-failure reliability demonstration needs ~229 trials: 9.2 years at 25 flights/yr, 2.3 years at 100/yr, 0.6 years at 400/yr. Robots help mostly through rapid reuse (robotic TPS inspection and tile replacement, pad refurbishment). That moves cadence milestones ~1-1.5 years earlier than S2 by 2031, but failures, pads, propellant and airspace still bind.

Construction-bound gates (pads, propellant plants, test facilities) compress less by 2031 (0.75-0.85x) than by 2035 (0.55-0.7x). About half of their schedule is long-lead equipment and permitting: large power transformers averaged ~128 weeks (Q2 2025), generator step-up units passed 160 weeks (Q1 2026). That supply chain must itself be robotized and expanded before it shortens. Starbase Pad 2 took ~16 months from flame-trench start to first launch (May 22, 2026), and is already a fast benchmark.

Off Earth, robots are the product, not the accelerant. Lunar construction and ISRU and in-space servicing and assembly are where S4 changes capability most, but they stay gated by landed mass, power (lunar reactor launch-ready late CY2029 target, 100 kWe), lunar-night survival, flight demonstrations and space-qualified actuators. OSAM-1 shows the risk: it grew from $626-753M to >$2B and was cancelled in March 2024. Northrop's MRV only launched on Jul 21, 2026.

Mars learning loops are fixed by orbital mechanics. Windows come every ~26 months. SpaceX skipped the late-2026 window (Feb 2026 pivot to the Moon), so at most 1-2 Mars iteration cycles fit by 2031 and 3-4 by 2035, whatever the robots. Lunar loops (opportunities every few days, ~3-5 day transit) are far faster, so S4's surface robotics will mature on the Moon first.

The robots-build-robots loop is fast enough by 2029-2030 to supply the space sector's labor needs in all three fleet scenarios: space needs ~10^5 robots, while even a slow 2-2.5x/yr ramp passes 1M fielded by ~2029. It is too slow to robotize the economy-scale supply chain (equipment makers, construction, fabs, mining) before ~2033-2035 in the base case. For space by 2031, robot quantity is not the binding variable. Robot capability at aerospace tolerances, requalification of robotic processes, and the non-labor gates are.

The evidence base for general-purpose robots doing real industrial work is thin as of Oct 2026. Humanoid shipments were ~13-18k in 2025 and ~19-22k in H1 2026, mostly Chinese makers and mostly research or education, with fewer than ~3-4k units on paid repeated work (secondary). Musk said in Jan 2026 that Optimus was not in material use in Tesla factories. Figure 02 at BMW ran 1,250+ hours of sheet-metal loading at a 5 mm tolerance over 11 months. Aerospace assembly needs tighter tolerances, torque and traceability records, and per-process qualification (AS9100/NADCAP, general).

Robotics also changes what sits on the critical path. Cheap parallel test articles make SpaceX-style hardware-rich iteration affordable for everyone. Parallel robotic labs collapse replicate statistics for allowables into the time of the longest single test. Robots on the Moon route around human rating for construction tasks. Robotic in-orbit assembly decouples structure size from fairing size, which matters for orbital-compute radiators.

gate_assessment.notes: Calendar-time factors (fraction of 2026 duration). Model S2/S3 values are from graph-v5.json domains.physclock.tables 'Physical gates'. Labor/physics/institution splits and all S4 factors are this study's estimates unless a source is named. The S4 2031 factor assumes robots reach leading firms (SpaceX, Rocket Lab, large primes, Chinese state and commercial firms) by 2028-2029 and the wider aerospace supply chain only after 2031.

rows.gate: Integration and test (vehicle and spacecraft; the model's 25% slice)
rows.today_2026: ~25% of a new system's critical path (model, general)
rows.split_labor_physics_institution: ~40% labor (assembly, harnessing, inspection, setup and teardown) / ~35% physics (test execution time constants) / ~25% queue and rework (facility availability, failure-driven serial loops)
rows.robotics_mechanism: Round-the-clock robotic integration and inspection; automated test setup; more parallel test articles; fewer workmanship escapes. Firefly's 2025 ground-test stage loss was a contamination process error during stage-one integration.
rows.cannot_compress: Physics-set test durations; serial rework after a failure; facility count

rows.gate: Environmental test campaign (thermal vacuum, vibration, acoustic, EMI)
rows.today_2026: Campaign 6-18 months (model); spacecraft-level TVAC ~2 weeks (Mars Express) to just over 2 months (Parker Solar Probe); GEVS minimums: 4 cycles at spacecraft level, 8 at component level, plateaus >=12 h, <1e-5 torr (NASA TFAWS 2026)
rows.split_labor_physics_institution: ~35% labor (fixtures, instrumentation, axis changes, teardown, anomaly troubleshooting) / ~40% physics (pump-down, transitions of a large thermal mass, dwells x cycles, sine and random durations) / ~25% queue and institution (chamber availability, readiness reviews, nonconformance dispositions)
rows.robotics_mechanism: 24/7 automated chamber operations, robotic instrumentation, faster axis changes, more chambers built
rows.cannot_compress: Dwell x cycle count: 4 cycles with >=12 h plateaus plus transitions is about a week minimum for a large spacecraft (general); the article's thermal time constant; workmanship screening by real cycling

rows.gate: Material and process qualification (creep, fatigue, corrosion in real time)
rows.today_2026: 10-20+ years for new materials; 1-3 years per additive machine and process (model). A standard 10,000-hour creep test runs ~14 months; a 10^7-cycle HCF test at 50-100 Hz takes 1-2.3 days per specimen (general)
rows.split_labor_physics_institution: ~20% labor (specimen machining, test tending, metallography, data reduction) / ~50% physics (real-time exposure, replicate statistics) / ~30% institution (allowables databases, NASA-STD-6030, MMPDS and CMH-17 acceptance, NASA-FAA CM4QC)
rows.robotics_mechanism: Robotic labs run 10-100x more specimens in parallel, so B- and A-basis replicate statistics finish within the window of the longest single test; closed-loop autonomous materials labs (the model dates autonomous labs at scale to 2028)
rows.S4_2035: 0.35-0.5x if accelerated testing plus model credit is accepted
rows.cannot_compress: The longest exposure the application needs (10^4-10^5 h creep, years of corrosion); extrapolation limits (Larson-Miller credit typically ~3x test time, general); acceleration valid only while the failure mechanism is unchanged; radiation dose-rate effects

rows.gate: Test stands and arc jets (capacity versus labor)
rows.today_2026: McGregor 15 stands (S-1). NASA's Ames Arc Jet Complex is the agency's sole ground facility for reentry TPS testing (NTRS 2024), built in the 1960s-70s and past its design life by 2010 (NASA 2010). Surveyed experts rank more arc jets the top hypersonic-materials test need (ETI via Air & Space Forces).
rows.model_S2_S3: Within 'Experiment and flight test' 1.1-1.3x / 1.3-1.5x speed (S3 already assumes AI-run test stands)
rows.split_labor_physics_institution: ~40% labor (model change, instrumentation, between-run turnaround, maintenance) / ~25% physics (run time, cooling, pump-down, electrode wear) / ~35% capital, power and institution (new facility construction, tens of MW, funding)
rows.robotics_mechanism: Automated model insertion and stand turnaround raise runs per day per facility ~1.3-1.8x (estimate); robots speed construction of new stands; cheap reentry flights (Starship, capsules) replace some ground runs
rows.cannot_compress: Arc-heater power and electrode life; facility capex; ground facilities cannot reproduce full reentry environments, so flight remains the final test

robots_build_robots_loop.starting_point: Humanoid shipments ~13k (Omdia) to ~18k (IDC) in 2025; ~19-22k in H1 2026; 2026 forecasts 50-100k (TrendForce >50k, SAG ~60k, Goldman 50-100k). Industrial robot stock 4.66M end-2024, 542k installed in 2024, stock growth ~9-11%/yr (IFR). The most recent doubling of the world robot stock took 6 years (Forethought).

scenarios.name: A Industrial ramp (2.5x/yr to 2028, 1.8x to 2031, 1.5x after)
B S4 base (3.5x/yr to 2029, 2x to 2031, 1.6x after)
C Retooled auto lines plus closed loop (4x/yr to 2029, then 3x, 2.5x, 2x...)
scenarios.fleet_2035: ~600M (likely capped by magnets, actuators and chips)

robots_build_robots_loop.assumptions: 2026 output 55k; 10%/yr attrition; a robot works ~5,000 h/yr vs ~1,900 for a human, at 0.3 (2028), 0.7 (2031) and 1.0 (2035) of human task productivity, i.e., ~0.8, ~1.8 and ~2.6 human-equivalents per robot (estimates).
robots_build_robots_loop.space_sector_need: If 30-50% of direct labor hours in global space manufacturing, test and launch operations (order 0.3-0.6M workers, general estimate; SpaceX alone >22,000 full-time employees as of Mar 31 2026 per its S-1) were robotized at ~1.8 human-equivalents per robot, space needs ~50k-170k robots. All three scenarios supply that by 2028-2029.
robots_build_robots_loop.economy_scale_need: Shortening the supply chain behind pads, propellant plants, test facilities and fabs (transformers, compressors, cryogenic equipment, steel, concrete, semiconductors) means robotizing a meaningful share of manufacturing and construction: order 10^7 robots plus redesigned factories. That arrives ~2031-2033 in B and ~2034-2036 in A.
robots_build_robots_loop.why_the_loop_is_not_the_early_driver: Through ~2030, humanoid output growth comes from human-built, retooled factories (Tesla converted Fremont's Model S/X lines to a 1M/yr design-capacity Optimus line, and a 10M/yr Giga Texas plant is planned; Figure BotQ is rated 12,000/yr), not from robots building robots. Forethought's estimate of ~1-year doublings for self-replicating robots on current technology (range 1-2 years; the appendix says 'a few years') means stock growth of ~2x/yr. That is slower than today's 3-4x/yr output growth from a tiny base, and it matters only once robots are a large share of manufacturing. FANUC has run robot-building-robot lines (unattended up to 30 days; capacity 5,000-6,000 robots/month in 2016-17) for two decades without runaway growth, because demand and non-robot inputs set the rate.
robots_build_robots_loop.binding_inputs_for_the_loop: Precision actuators (roller screws, harmonic reducers), rare-earth magnets (China-dominated, export-controlled, general), inference chips (SpaceX's S-1 says Terafab will make chips for Optimus), batteries, factory buildings and power
robots_build_robots_loop.verdict_2031_vs_2035: By 2031 the loop matters for space only inside leading firms and as the off-Earth workforce. Robot quantity is not the binding variable. Capability at aerospace tolerances, process requalification and the non-labor gates are. By 2035 (scenario B) the loop matters for the supply chain and construction, which is where most of the extra S4 compression between 2031 and 2035 comes from.

physics_time_constants_and_hard_limits: Thermal vacuum: >=4 cycles at spacecraft level, >=12 h plateaus (GEVS via NASA TFAWS 2026); large spacecraft need days to stabilize thermally (general)
Creep: 10^4 h (~14 months) standard tests; 10^5 h (~11.4 years) for long-life allowables; extrapolation credit typically ~3x test time (general)
Fatigue: 10^7 cycles at 50-100 Hz takes 1-2.3 days per specimen; thermomechanical fatigue runs minutes per cycle, so weeks per specimen (general)
Concrete reaches design strength at 28 days (general)
Reliability: n = ln(1-C)/ln(R), ~229 zero-failure trials for R=0.99 at C=0.90
Mars synodic period ~26 months; transit ~6-9 months; lunar night ~14.75 days; lunar opportunities every few days with ~3-5 day transits (general; SpaceX Feb 2026 rationale)
Propellant: 5,250 t per Starship stack; merchant supply needs ~389 tanker movements per flight; power and gas bind only near 10,000 flights/yr (Mach33)
Long-lead electrical equipment: large power transformers ~128 weeks (Q2 2025); generator step-up >160 weeks (Q1 2026) (Wood Mackenzie via press)

quantitative_anchors.value: 57-63% shorter by 2031 (S3 51%); 66-74% by 2035; floor 78% (4.6x) with infinite robots and cognition

what_robotics_compresses: Labor-bound factory steps: machine tending, welding, stacking, harnessing, TPS tile and pin installation, inspection (engine and vehicle time-to-rate 0.5-0.7x by 2031, 0.35-0.55x by 2035)
Test setup, teardown, instrumentation, axis changes and 24/7 chamber and stand operations (environmental campaigns 0.6-0.7x by 2031, 0.45-0.6x by 2035)
Facility queues and capacity: more runs per day per stand or arc jet, plus more facilities built (0.6-0.75x by 2031, 0.4-0.6x by 2035)
Replicate statistics for materials and component allowables, by running 10-100x more specimens in parallel (material and process qualification 0.45-0.6x by 2031)
Refurbishment and turnaround labor for reuse (robotic TPS inspection and tile replacement), which raises flight cadence and so speeds statistics-bound gates indirectly
Construction site labor for pads, propellant plants and test facilities (0.75-0.85x by 2031, 0.55-0.7x by 2035)
Workmanship escapes, such as Firefly's 2025 contamination error during stage integration
Cost of test articles, making hardware-rich parallel iteration affordable beyond SpaceX
Off-Earth work: lunar site preparation, ISRU operations, in-space servicing and assembly, where robots are the workforce and S4 changes capability more than speed
Hardware unit cost at robot-adopting lines (~10-25% by 2031, ~25-45% by 2035, estimates)
what_robotics_cannot_compress: Physics time constants: thermal-vacuum dwells and cycles, a spacecraft's thermal time constant, creep and corrosion exposure (10^4-10^5 h), concrete cure, curing and densification cycles, hot-fire and burn durations
Failure discovery that happens only in hot fire or flight, and the serial build-fly-learn loop that waits on each result
Statistical evidence: ~229 zero-failure trials for 0.99/90%; flight-level trials accrue only at launch cadence
Orbital mechanics: Mars windows every ~26 months (at most 1-2 iterations by 2031, 3-4 by 2035) and transit times
Lunar environment: ~14.75-day night, dust, thermal cycling, surface power (reactor launch-ready ~late 2029 target), landed mass per year
Institutional clocks: FAA Part 450 statutory review, NEPA comment and litigation, ITU coordination, human-rating boards, NSPM-20 nuclear launch approval, appropriations

Long-lead equipment and supply capacity: transformers (~128-160+ weeks), cryogenic plants, rad-hard fab capacity, single sources, export controls, until those industries are themselves robotized (mostly after 2031)
Requalification of robotized processes (AS9100, NADCAP, weld procedure and first-article requalification), ~6-24 months per process per supplier (estimate)
Energy and materials at extreme cadence: propellant plants and gas supply (bind near 10,000 flights/yr), plus magnets, actuators and chips for the robots themselves
timeline_view: 2026-2028: robots enter leading space factories on top of automation that already exists (Starfactory, Redmond, Rosie and AFP lines). Humanoid output ramps from ~55k (2026) toward 0.2-0.9M/yr, but useful aerospace-grade work is limited, so S4 is effectively S3 for space; cadence stays gated by Starship development, pads and propellant. 2029-2031: robot capability (S3 cognition) and supply (1-26M/yr output across scenarios) are enough for leading firms to robotize I&T, test operations, refurbishment and in-house fabrication. The new-program Amdahl ceiling rises from 51% to ~57-63% shorter, and realized gains reach ~40-50% vs 35-45% in S3. Starship cadence milestones arrive ~1-1.5 years ahead of S2. The first robotic lunar construction and ISRU pilots and routine GEO servicing happen, while Mars allows at most 1-2 learning cycles. The wider supply chain, construction and licensing barely change. 2031-2035: in scenario B (~16M robots by 2031, ~140M by 2035) suppliers, equipment makers and construction robotize. Pads, propellant plants, test facilities and long-lead parts compress to ~0.55-0.75x, and the ceiling reaches ~66-74% (realized ~50-62%). Lunar construction scales if Starship lunar cargo reaches ~10+ landings/yr. Beyond 2035 the floor is ~78% shorter (4.6x), set by physics, statistics, windows and institutions. The robots-build-robots loop matters for space mainly after 2031, through the supply chain and construction, not through the factories, which robots saturate early.
strongest_case_fast: S3 cognition solves robot dexterity and autonomy by 2027-2028. Retooled auto lines (Fremont's 1M/yr design capacity, a planned 10M/yr Giga Texas plant, BotQ's 12,000/yr line going 24x in four months) push humanoid output 4x/yr to tens of millions by 2031. SpaceX already has robotic welding, cutting and TPS installation, ~$100B of cash and an affiliated robot maker. It robotizes Starbase, Gigabay, McGregor and Florida refurbishment by 2028-29. Robotic tile inspection and replacement unlocks rapid reuse, so Starship reaches hundreds of flights/yr by 2030. At 400 flights/yr a 229-trial reliability case takes ~7 months, collapsing reuse-learning, reliability and much of human-rating evidence. Parallel robotic labs finish allowables in the time of one long test; regulators accept model-plus-accelerated-test credit (S3 dates regulator credit to 2029). Robotic crews build the Louisiana campus and more arc jets on 2-3 shift-equivalents. Starship-delivered robots and a 2029-30 reactor start a lunar outpost, and orbital-compute radiators are assembled in orbit. Then the 2031 compression is at the top of the range (~63% shorter for new programs, realized ~50%). Throughput (vehicles, satellites, pads, tests per year) rises by roughly an order of magnitude by 2035, and in this case even the 2035 ceiling (~74%) is reached early.
strongest_case_slow: The record shows automation multiplying individual steps without multiplying cadence. Rocket Lab's ~33x robot step became ~3.5x launches over six years. Relativity's printing-first factory flew once and failed, and it reverted to welded aluminum. Firefly's automated composites coexist with ~1-3 launches a year. Neutron slipped despite a 90-t AFP robot. Starship cadence (5 flights in 2025, 3 in 2026 to Oct 7) is set by failures and pads, with vehicles already ahead of flights. General-purpose robots are not yet doing material industrial work: Optimus by Musk's own Jan 2026 account, and fewer than ~3-4k humanoids on paid repeated work worldwide. Aerospace adoption is slowed by tolerances, traceability and process requalification at every supplier. FANUC's 20-year-old robots-build-robots lines never produced runaway growth. Half of pad and plant schedules are transformers (128-160+ weeks), cryogenic equipment and permits. Licensing, human rating and nuclear approval are untouched; physics time constants, statistics and 26-month Mars windows are untouched; and the lunar reactor program has a history of slips. On this view S4 adds only ~3-6 points to S3 by 2031 (realized ~38-45%). Robotics matters for space mainly after 2033, via the supply chain, and the ~78% floor binds well before the robots-build-robots loop does.
implications_for_the_tree: Add S4 as a fourth column with the class multipliers above. Treat 2031 S4 as S3 plus ~5-13 points on the Amdahl ceiling, not a regime change.

Separate throughput nodes (production rate, test capacity, construction crews, replicate statistics), which S4 compresses, from latency nodes (dwells, real-time exposure, flight learning, windows, statutory clocks), which it does not.
Re-date nodes gated by refurbishment labor (Starship rapid reuse, 100+ flights/yr) ~1-1.5 years earlier than S2 under S4. Nodes gated by flight count follow from the cadence change.
Treat lunar construction, ISRU and in-space servicing and assembly as robotics-capability nodes. S4 moves them most, but landed mass, power and flight demos bind.
Add a node 'robotic process requalification standard' (AS9100, NADCAP, customer acceptance of robot-made flight hardware) as the institutional gate on S4 adoption in aerospace.

Signposts: Optimus or Figure units doing paid aerospace assembly; SpaceX disclosing robot counts at Starbase or McGregor; Starship booster and ship turnaround under 1 week; arc-jet runs per day doubling; transformer lead times falling below 80 weeks; first lunar regolith pad built robotically.
